stem: An analyst drags the string field `Genre` to Rows. What does Tableau draw for it?

options.text: A vertical axis with tick marks running from the lowest to the highest genre
options.rationale: Axes belong to continuous fields. A string field has no number line, so it cannot get one.

options.text: A color gradient legend that shades each genre from low to high
options.rationale: Gradients are what a continuous field gets on Color, and `Genre` is not on Color here.

options.text: One row header for each genre in the data
options.rationale: The field is discrete, so it makes a separate, distinct label for every member, like a pivot table row label.

options.text: A single combined row that adds up all genres into one mark
options.rationale: Putting a dimension on Rows splits the view by its members instead of combining them.

explanation: Discrete fields are blue and draw headers, one per member. Continuous fields draw axes. A string dimension such as `Genre` is always discrete.

stem: A view has the discrete field `Type` on Color. What does the legend show?

options.text: A distinct color for each member of `Type`
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color gets a categorical palette: one color per member, listed in a legend.

options.text: A gradient bar that runs from the smallest to the largest `Type`
options.rationale: A gradient (quantitative legend) is for continuous fields, and `Type` is discrete here.

options.text: One shade of a single color, darker for members with more rows
options.rationale: Shading by size or count of members is how a continuous measure behaves, not a discrete field.

options.text: No legend, because discrete fields on Color are drawn as headers
options.rationale: Headers appear on Rows and Columns. On Color, discrete fields get a legend.

explanation: The Color shelf follows the same rule as the shelves: discrete means separate members, so each gets its own color. Continuous means a range, so it gets a gradient.

stem: In a view, the `Release Year` pill on Columns was made continuous and now draws an axis of years. The analyst wants one header per year instead. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Change the aggregation of `Release Year` to Count (Distinct)
options.rationale: This changes the pill to an aggregated measure value, which does not give a header for each year.

options.text: Drag `Release Year` onto the Detail card on the Marks card
options.rationale: Detail changes the level of detail of the marks but does not draw headers.

options.text: Right-click `Release Year` in the Data pane and choose Create > Group
options.rationale: A group makes a new field that combines members. It does not change how the field is displayed.

options.text: Switch the `Release Year` pill back to discrete from its right-click menu
options.rationale: Making the pill discrete turns it blue, so it draws a header for each year.

explanation: A numeric dimension can be discrete or continuous. A discrete pill draws headers, a continuous one an axis. The pill's right-click menu switches it for this view only.

stem: An analyst right-clicks the green `SUM(Minutes Watched)` pill on Columns and chooses Convert to Discrete. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The pill becomes a dimension and is no longer aggregated
options.rationale: Converting to discrete does not turn a measure into a dimension.

options.text: The field is still a measure and still aggregated, but now draws headers
options.rationale: Continuity and role are separate properties. Making a measure discrete changes the display, not the role.

options.text: The pill stays green, because measures are always continuous
options.rationale: Measures can be discrete or continuous. A discrete pill is blue.

options.text: The pill still draws an axis, but with whole-number ticks only
options.rationale: A discrete pill draws headers instead of an axis.

explanation: Blue/green (continuity) is a different question from dimension/measure (role). A blue measure is still aggregated.

stem: Which Driftlight field can NOT be made continuous?

options.text: `Release Year`, a numeric dimension
options.rationale: Numeric dimensions can be discrete or continuous.

options.text: `Country`, a string dimension
options.rationale: Strings and Booleans have no number line, so Tableau offers no continuous option for them.

options.text: `Start`, a date dimension
options.rationale: Date dimensions can be discrete or continuous.

options.text: `Minutes Watched`, a measure
options.rationale: All measures can be discrete or continuous.

explanation: Tableau's help says date and numeric dimensions can be discrete or continuous, and all measures can too. String and Boolean dimensions cannot be continuous.

stem: An analyst puts the measure `Minutes Watched` on Color in a view of genres. What does the color legend look like?

options.text: A list with one fixed color per genre
options.rationale: That is a categorical palette, which a discrete field gets.

options.text: A list with one fixed color per distinct minute value
options.rationale: A continuous field does not break into one color per value.

options.text: No legend, because measures cannot be placed on Color
options.rationale: Measures can go on Color. The legend is a gradient.

options.text: A gradient from low to high values
options.rationale: Continuous fields on Color get a quantitative legend with a continuous range of colors.

explanation: A continuous field on Color shows a gradient so any value in between has a place on the color scale.

stem: A view contains a green pill on Columns. What does Tableau draw for it?

options.text: An axis, a range with tick marks
options.rationale: Green means continuous, and continuous fields draw an axis.

options.text: A header for each member, with a label above each column
options.rationale: Headers are drawn for discrete (blue) pills.

options.text: A categorical legend with one color per member
options.rationale: Legends belong to the Color shelf, and a green pill on Columns draws an axis.

options.text: A table of the individual records behind the marks
options.rationale: Showing records is a different feature and not linked to pill color.

explanation: Continuous pills create axes with a minimum, a maximum and tick marks, where any value in between has a place.

stem: In a worksheet, an analyst right-clicks the `Release Year` pill on Columns and chooses Convert to Continuous. What happens to the `Release Year` field in the Data pane?

options.text: It also turns green and becomes continuous in every worksheet
options.rationale: Only the pill in the view changes.

options.text: It moves from Dimensions to Measures, because it is now continuous
options.rationale: Continuity does not change the field's role, so it stays a dimension.

options.text: Nothing: it stays discrete, and only this view changes
options.rationale: Converting a pill affects that view only. The field in the Data pane keeps its default.

options.text: It is removed from the Data pane and replaced by a copy
options.rationale: Converting a pill does not copy or remove the field.

explanation: There are two places to switch continuity: the field in the Data pane, or a pill in one view. The pill's change stays in that view.

stem: How does an analyst make the `Release Year` field continuous for every new view?

options.text: Drag the field from the Dimensions area into the Measures area
options.rationale: Moving a field between areas is about its role, not its continuity, and does not make it continuous.

options.text: Change the aggregation of the field to Sum in a view
options.rationale: Aggregation does not set blue or green for a field in the Data pane.

options.text: Change its default number format under Default Properties
options.rationale: Number format changes how values are written, not whether the field is discrete or continuous.

options.text: Right-click the field in the Data pane and choose Convert to Continuous
options.rationale: The Data pane menu changes the field itself, so new pills start out green.

explanation: Use Convert to Discrete or Convert to Continuous, either on the Data pane field or on a pill in the view.

stem: The marketing team asks whether Driftlight viewing is higher in certain months of the year, whichever year it is. Which pill suits this question?

options.text: The continuous date value `MONTH(Start)`
options.rationale: A date value keeps the year, so January 2024 and January 2025 stay apart on a timeline.

options.text: The discrete date part `MONTH(Start)`
options.rationale: A date part merges the same month of every year into one of 12 headers, which shows seasonality.

options.text: The continuous date value `YEAR(Start)`
options.rationale: This shows one point per year and has no month-level pattern.

options.text: The Exact Date level of `Start`
options.rationale: Exact Date gives one member per distinct date-time, far more detailed than months.

explanation: Date parts answer "which month is busiest in any year?" Date values answer "how did viewing change over time?"

stem: Finance wants a line that follows Driftlight viewing month by month across 2024 and 2025. Which pill goes on Columns?

options.text: The continuous (green) date value `MONTH(Start)`
options.rationale: It keeps the year, so the line runs through the months in order and shows the trend.

options.text: The discrete (blue) date part `MONTH(Start)`
options.rationale: It would merge both years into 12 headers, hiding the trend across years.

options.text: The discrete date part `YEAR(Start)` only
options.rationale: It gives a header per year, with no month-level detail.

options.text: A continuous measure `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns
options.rationale: A measure is not a date and does not lay out months in time order.

explanation: The continuous date value sits in the lower, continuous section of the date menu and draws a timeline.

stem: An analyst drags a date field spanning several years to Columns. Which level does Tableau pick by default?

options.text: MONTH, because it is the most common level
options.rationale: MONTH is the default only when the data covers a single year.

options.text: Exact Date, because it is the most detailed
options.rationale: Exact Date is a choice from the menu, not the default.

options.text: YEAR, the level with multiple instances
options.rationale: Tableau picks the level at which there are multiple instances. With several years, that is YEAR.

options.text: QUARTER, as the middle level between year and month
options.rationale: Tableau does not choose a middle level by default.

explanation: The default depends on the data: several years of data gives YEAR, a single year gives MONTH.

stem: A view shows the discrete pill `YEAR(Start)`. The analyst clicks its + control. What happens?

options.text: The pill is converted to a continuous date value
options.rationale: Converting needs the pill menu. The + control only drills.

options.text: Tableau adds the year before to the filter
options.rationale: The + control does not filter.

options.text: The pill changes to the Exact Date level
options.rationale: Drilling steps down one level at a time.

options.text: Tableau drills down and adds `QUARTER(Start)` next to it
options.rationale: The plus control drills into the next level of the date hierarchy: quarter, then month, and so on.

explanation: Discrete date pills can be drilled with a +, which adds the next level of detail beside them.

stem: Which statements about discrete fields are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Their pills are blue
options.rationale: Blue marks a discrete field.

options.text: On Rows or Columns they draw headers, one per member
options.rationale: Headers are how discrete fields are displayed.

options.text: On Rows or Columns they draw an axis with tick marks
options.rationale: Axes belong to continuous fields.

options.text: On Color they get a gradient legend
options.rationale: Gradients are for continuous fields. Discrete fields get a palette.

options.text: Only dimensions can be discrete
options.rationale: Measures can also be discrete, and then they draw headers.

explanation: Discrete fields are blue and draw headers. Dimensions are often discrete but measures can be too.

stem: Which three view choices make Tableau draw headers rather than an axis? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: `Genre` on Rows
options.rationale: A string dimension is discrete, so it draws headers.

options.text: The date part `MONTH(Start)` on Columns
options.rationale: A date part is discrete and gives 12 headers.

options.text: `Release Year` converted to discrete on Columns
options.rationale: A discrete numeric dimension gives a header per year.

options.text: The date value `MONTH(Start)` on Columns
options.rationale: A date value is continuous and draws a timeline axis.

options.text: `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Rows with its default continuity
options.rationale: A measure is continuous by default and draws an axis.

options.text: `Release Year` converted to continuous on Columns
options.rationale: Continuous draws an axis of years.

explanation: Headers come from blue pills: string dimensions, date parts and fields converted to discrete.

stem: Which two Driftlight fields can be continuous? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `Start`, a date field
options.rationale: Date dimensions can be discrete or continuous.

options.text: `Minutes Watched`, a measure
options.rationale: All measures can be discrete or continuous.

options.text: `Genre`, a string field
options.rationale: Strings can't be continuous.

options.text: `Country`, a string field
options.rationale: Strings can't be continuous.

options.text: A field containing only True or False values
options.rationale: Booleans can't be continuous.

explanation: Only dates, numbers and measures can be continuous. Strings and Booleans cannot.

stem: Which two statements describe the date value `MONTH(Start)`, in the continuous section of the date menu? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Its pill is green and draws an axis
options.rationale: Date values are continuous.

options.text: January 2024 and January 2025 stay separate points
options.rationale: A date value keeps the year, so each month of each year is its own point.

options.text: It merges the same month of every year
options.rationale: That describes the date part.

options.text: It draws 12 headers from January to December
options.rationale: That is the date part, which is discrete.

options.text: It turns the date field into a measure
options.rationale: The role stays a dimension.

explanation: A date value is a truncated date, a position on a timeline, so it suits trends.

stem: Which three statements about discrete date parts are true? (Choose 3 answers.)

options.text: The pill is blue
options.rationale: Date parts are discrete.

options.text: `MONTH(Start)` as a part adds up the same month across all years
options.rationale: A part merges everything but that part of the date.

options.text: It suits questions about seasonality
options.rationale: Months from all years share one header, so seasonal patterns stand out.

options.text: It draws a continuous timeline with one point for each month
options.rationale: That is the date value.

options.text: It keeps January 2024 separate from January 2025
options.rationale: The part drops the year.

options.text: It turns the date field into a measure
options.rationale: Dates stay dimensions.

explanation: A date part is like `EXTRACT(MONTH FROM start)`: one part of the date. A date value is like `DATE_TRUNC`.

stem: In the chart, `Genre` is on Rows and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` is on Columns. How are the two fields drawn?

options.text: `Genre` gets an axis with tick marks, and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` gets one header per value
options.rationale: The roles are reversed. A string field has no number line, so it cannot draw an axis.

options.text: Both fields get headers, because every pill on Rows or Columns draws headers
options.rationale: Only discrete fields draw headers. A continuous pill draws an axis.

options.text: `Genre` gets a header for each member, and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` gets an axis
options.rationale: `Genre` is discrete (blue), so it draws headers. The summed measure is continuous (green), so it draws a numeric axis.

options.text: Both fields get axes, because the bars need a number line in both directions
options.rationale: A discrete field never draws an axis. The bars sit in one pane per genre instead.

explanation: Discrete (blue) fields draw headers with a separate label per member. Continuous (green) fields draw an axis with a continuous range. Here the string `Genre` is discrete and the summed measure is continuous.

stem: The shelves show two blue pills on Rows, `Genre` and `Type`. What will Tableau draw for them?

options.text: Header labels for both fields, with the `Type` headers sitting inside each `Genre` header
options.rationale: Both pills are discrete, so both draw headers. The pill listed second is nested inside the first.

options.text: A numeric axis for `Genre` and a separate set of headers for `Type`
options.rationale: A string field cannot draw an axis. Both pills are blue and draw headers.

options.text: A single axis for the two fields, with the genres and types shown as tick marks
options.rationale: Tick marks on an axis belong to continuous fields. Discrete members get header labels.

options.text: Header labels for `Genre` only, because Tableau draws headers for just the first discrete pill
options.rationale: Every discrete pill on Rows or Columns draws its own headers.

explanation: Each discrete pill on Rows or Columns draws headers, one per member. With two discrete pills the headers nest, much like the row labels of a pivot table.

stem: The chart shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` by `Genre`, with `Type` on Color. Which statements are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: `Genre` is discrete, so there is one header per genre
options.rationale: A string dimension on Rows is blue and draws headers.

options.text: `Type` on Color is drawn as a gradient from low to high
options.rationale: A gradient is for continuous fields. `Type` is a discrete string field.

options.text: `SUM(Minutes Watched)` is discrete, so it draws a header for every value
options.rationale: The summed measure is continuous here, so it draws an axis.

options.text: The legend lists a separate color for each member of `Type`
options.rationale: A discrete field on Color gets a categorical palette with one entry per member.

options.text: Moving `Genre` to Color would give it a gradient legend
options.rationale: `Genre` is still discrete on Color. It would get a color per genre, not a gradient.

explanation: Discrete fields draw headers on Rows and Columns and a categorical palette on Color. Gradients and axes belong to continuous fields.

stem: The shelves show `Plan` on Columns and a blue `SUM(Minutes Watched)` pill on Rows. What does the blue pill mean for the view?

options.text: The measure becomes a dimension and is no longer summed
options.rationale: Making a measure discrete does not change its role. It is still aggregated.

options.text: Tableau draws a numeric axis with a continuous range of summed values
options.rationale: An axis belongs to continuous pills. A blue pill draws headers.

options.text: Tableau hides the field and draws only the `Plan` headers
options.rationale: A blue pill is still part of the view. It just uses headers instead of an axis.

options.text: It is still summed, but each distinct sum gets a header
options.rationale: Discrete is a display property. The aggregation stays, and each separate value becomes a header label.

explanation: Discrete versus continuous is separate from dimension versus measure. A measure converted to discrete is still a measure and is still aggregated, but it draws headers instead of an axis.

stem: The chart shows one bar per `Genre`. What is true of the bars' positions across the view?

options.text: Each bar is placed along a number line according to the value of its genre
options.rationale: `Genre` is a string with no numeric value, so it has no place on a number line.

options.text: Each bar sits under its own header, and there is no position between two genres
options.rationale: Discrete members are separate and distinct, so the view has labelled headers with nothing in between.

options.text: The bars are placed on a continuous axis, with the genre names as its tick marks
options.rationale: Tick marks on a continuous axis mark values on an unbroken range, which genres do not have.

options.text: The bars are merged into one wide pane until the analyst adds a field to Color
options.rationale: Headers split the view by member already. Color is not needed for that.

explanation: A discrete field makes separate, distinct members. Tableau draws one header per member, and the view has no in-between values.

stem: The chart counts titles by release year. The `Release Year` pill on Columns is green and the view shows an axis of years. What produced the axis?

options.text: `Release Year` was changed from a dimension to a measure in the view
options.rationale: The role is unchanged. Release Year stays a dimension, and only its continuity changed.

options.text: `Release Year` was aggregated with `SUM`, which makes a pill green
options.rationale: The pill reads `Release Year`, not `SUM(Release Year)`, so nothing was aggregated. Its colour comes from its continuity.

options.text: The pill was converted to continuous, so it draws an axis
options.rationale: A numeric dimension can be discrete or continuous. Continuous pills are green and draw an axis.

options.text: `Titles (Count)` was moved from Rows over to the Columns shelf
options.rationale: Moving a different pill would not change how `Release Year` is drawn.

explanation: Numeric and date dimensions can be discrete or continuous. Converting `Release Year` to continuous gives a green pill and an axis of years, but the field stays a dimension.

stem: The shelves show a continuous `Release Year` pill on Columns and `AVG(Runtime)` on Rows. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both are green and draw axes, though `Release Year` is a dimension
options.rationale: Continuity and role are separate. A numeric dimension can be continuous.

options.text: `Release Year` must be a measure now, because only measures are green
options.rationale: Colour shows continuity, not role. A dimension can be green.

options.text: Only `AVG(Runtime)` draws an axis, because `Release Year` is a dimension
options.rationale: A continuous dimension draws an axis too, like any green pill.

options.text: Both pills draw headers, because an average is a discrete value
options.rationale: Averages of numbers are continuous by default and draw an axis.

explanation: Green pills draw axes, whether the field is a dimension or a measure. A numeric dimension such as `Release Year` can be converted to continuous without becoming a measure.

stem: The chart shows `Genre` on Rows and `SUM(Minutes Watched)` on Columns, with `SUM(Minutes Watched)` also on Color. Which statements are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The Color legend shows a distinct color for each genre
options.rationale: Genre is on Rows, not Color. The legend belongs to the continuous measure.

options.text: The Color legend is a gradient from low to high values
options.rationale: A continuous field on Color gets a quantitative legend.

options.text: The Color pill is blue, because it is a measure
options.rationale: Measures are green by default, and colour shows continuity, not role.

options.text: `Minutes Watched` on Color turned into a dimension
options.rationale: Putting a measure on Color doesn't change its role. It is still an aggregated measure.

options.text: The color of each bar follows its summed value
options.rationale: The shading steps through the range, so bars with larger sums get a different shade than smaller ones.

explanation: A continuous field on Color is shown as a gradient, so each mark is shaded according to its value. A discrete field would get a separate color per member instead.

stem: The chart shows a continuous timeline with `YEAR(Start)` as a date value. The analyst wants one header per year instead of an axis. What should they change?

options.text: Convert `Minutes Watched` on Rows to a discrete pill
options.rationale: That changes the Rows pill. The Columns pill would still draw an axis.

options.text: Drag `Start` from Columns to the Color shelf instead
options.rationale: Color doesn't add headers, and the timeline would be removed.

options.text: Change `Start` from a dimension to a measure
options.rationale: Role doesn't decide between headers and an axis; continuity does, and the date part or value choice sets it.

options.text: Pick the discrete date part `YEAR(Start)` in the menu
options.rationale: Date parts are discrete and draw headers, one per year. Date values are continuous and draw an axis.

explanation: The date menu offers each level as a discrete part and a continuous value. Choosing the part turns the pill blue and draws headers instead of a timeline.

stem: The shelves show `Genre` on Rows, `Titles (Count)` on Columns, and a green `Release Year` pill on Color. What will the Color legend look like?

options.text: A list with a separate color for each release year
options.rationale: That is what a discrete pill on Color gets. This pill is green.

options.text: A gradient running from earlier to later years
options.rationale: A continuous field on Color gets a quantitative legend, even though `Release Year` is a dimension.

options.text: No legend, because a dimension on Color doesn't get one
options.rationale: Any field on Color gets a legend. Dimensions get one too.

options.text: A gradient of counts, because Color always shows the measure
options.rationale: Color shows the field placed on it. Here that is `Release Year`, not the count.

explanation: The legend follows the pill's continuity. A green `Release Year` gets a gradient, and a blue one would get a color per year.

stem: The chart shows a timeline with one point per month across the two years. The analyst wants 12 headers, January to December, to look for seasonality. What should they change?

options.text: Switch `MONTH(Start)` to the discrete date part
options.rationale: A date part is discrete, so the headers appear and each month's two years add together.

options.text: Convert `Minutes Watched` on Rows to a discrete pill
options.rationale: That changes the Rows pill. The Columns pill would still be a timeline.

options.text: Replace the field `Start` with `Sessions (Count)`
options.rationale: That removes the date from the view, so there is no seasonality to compare.

options.text: Add `YEAR(Start)` to Color, which splits the lines by year
options.rationale: Color splits the lines by year, but the axis stays a timeline with all months in it.

explanation: Date values are continuous and keep the year. Date parts are discrete and merge the same month of every year, which suits seasonality.

stem: Finance wants to see whether viewing is growing across 2024 and 2025. Why doesn't this chart answer that?

options.text: `SUM(Minutes Watched)` should be an average so that growth shows up
options.rationale: The aggregation isn't the problem. Averaging wouldn't restore the years.

options.text: Month headers are only suited to bar charts, never to trends
options.rationale: Headers can be shown in any chart. The issue is what the date pill does to the years.

options.text: The pill is a date value, so it hides the difference between months
options.rationale: A date value would keep every month in order. This pill is a blue part.

options.text: `MONTH(Start)` is a date part, so each month adds up both years
options.rationale: A date part merges the years. A continuous date value would keep a timeline.

explanation: A discrete date part such as `MONTH(Start)` combines all years into 12 headers. For a trend over time, use the continuous date value so the two years run one after the other.

stem: The shelves show a blue `MONTH(Start)` pill on Columns. Which statements are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Each header adds up that month across every year in the data
options.rationale: A date part keeps only the month, so the same month of different years falls together.

options.text: The view draws a continuous timeline in month order
options.rationale: A timeline comes from a green date value. This pill is blue.

options.text: The pill is a date part, listed in the upper, discrete section of its menu
options.rationale: Date parts are the discrete choices, and date values are in the continuous section.

options.text: The pill is a date value that truncates the date to the month
options.rationale: Date values, or truncated dates, are green.

options.text: The view has a separate point for January 2024 and January 2025
options.rationale: That needs a date value. A date part gives one header for January.

explanation: Blue date pills are date parts: discrete headers that merge years. Green date pills are date values: a continuous timeline.

stem: The chart shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` with the date parts `YEAR(Start)` and `QUARTER(Start)` on Columns. Which statements are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: Both date pills are discrete, so they draw headers
options.rationale: Date parts are blue and draw headers.

options.text: Both date pills are continuous, so they draw one shared axis
options.rationale: An axis needs green date values. These are discrete parts.

options.text: The quarter headers repeat under each year
options.rationale: The year is the first header, so the quarters are listed again inside each of them.

options.text: Tableau merges the quarters into four headers shared by all years
options.rationale: That happens only when `YEAR(Start)` isn't in the view.

options.text: Replacing both with date values would still draw headers
options.rationale: Date values are continuous and draw an axis instead.

explanation: Discrete date parts draw nested headers, like any discrete fields. The quarter part is split by year only because the year is also in the view.

stem: The shelves show a green `QUARTER(Start)` pill on Columns. How does it differ from the blue date part `QUARTER(Start)`?

options.text: It is a date part, so it draws four headers instead of an axis
options.rationale: Date parts are blue. A green date pill is a date value.

options.text: It keeps the year, so quarters run in time order
options.rationale: A date value is truncated to the quarter and stays continuous, so each year has its own quarters.

options.text: It adds the same quarter of every year, giving four marks
options.rationale: That is what the discrete date part does, not the date value.

options.text: It is a measure, so Tableau sums its values for each mark
options.rationale: The pill is still a date dimension, and colour shows continuity, not role.

explanation: A date value is the actual date truncated to a level, such as Q1 2024. It is continuous and ordered in time, while the date part merges years.

stem: The chart shows `SUM(Minutes Watched)` by the green date value `QUARTER(Start)`. Which statements are correct? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The quarters of both years run in sequence along one timeline
options.rationale: A date value is truncated to the quarter, so each year keeps its own quarters.

options.text: All first quarters are merged into a single point
options.rationale: Merging is what a discrete date part does.

options.text: The pill is a dimension, even though it is green
options.rationale: Colour shows continuity. The date field stays a dimension.

options.text: The view shows a header for each quarter
options.rationale: Headers come from discrete pills. This pill draws an axis.

options.text: The pill changed `Start` into a measure
options.rationale: Choosing a date value changes continuity and level. It doesn't change the role.

explanation: Green date values form a continuous, ordered timeline. They are still dimensions, and they keep the year, unlike discrete date parts.
